summary.text: Metamorphic rocks form when an existing rock is turned into a new kind of rock by heat and often pressure, while staying mostly solid.
The starting rock can be igneous, sedimentary or already metamorphic, and the change can come from deep burial, continental collisions or heating by nearby magma.
Because each mineral is stable only within certain limits, the minerals in a metamorphic rock show roughly the temperatures and pressures it went through.

facts.label: Examples
facts.value: Gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite

facts.label: Early insight
facts.value: James Hutton linked them to great heat in 1795

items.prompt: A bed of limestone is buried deep and heated for a long time, but never melts. What rock does it most likely become?
items.explain: During metamorphism the small calcite crystals in limestone grow into larger crystals, producing marble.

items.prompt: James Hall sealed chalk inside a cannon barrel and heated it in a foundry furnace. What came out?
items.explain: Sealed under pressure, the chalk became something strongly resembling marble, not the quicklime that chalk gives when heated in open air.

items.prompt: Kyanite, andalusite and sillimanite share exactly the same chemical formula, yet each forms at a different temperature. What does this show about metamorphism?

options.label: Rocks must melt before minerals can change
Minerals can change with no change in chemistry
New minerals always need fluids bringing new elements
Temperature has no effect on which minerals form

items.explain: All three are Al₂SiO₅; kyanite turns to andalusite and then sillimanite as temperature rises, so the mineral changes without the bulk composition changing.

items.prompt: A rock is heated until it melts completely, then cools and hardens again. What kind of rock is it now?
items.explain: Rock that forms from molten magma is igneous; metamorphic rock changes without melting to any great degree.

items.prompt: Geologists study metamorphic rocks lying at the surface to learn about conditions far underground. Why does this work?

options.label: Surface rocks share today's deep temperatures
Their minerals record past heat and pressure
They hold trapped air from deep inside the Earth
Their colors change with the weather above them

items.explain: These rocks were exposed by erosion and uplift, and their minerals indicate the temperatures and pressures at which they were metamorphosed.

items.prompt: Engineers planning a tunnel learn the bedrock is schist. Why might they worry?

options.label: It is far too hard to drill
It has pronounced planes of weakness

items.explain: Schist bedrock can challenge civil engineering because of its pronounced planes of weakness.
